note: Billionaire Life prototype. Every date and number below appears in at least one cited source. Situations and outcomes are summarized in our own words and simplified. Alternatives are generic choices for the game, not claims about what he considered.

person.name: Jeff Bezos
person.role: Founder and Executive Chair of Amazon
person.bio: Founded Amazon in 1994 and has chaired its board ever since. He was CEO from May 1996 to July 2021, then became Executive Chair. He also founded Blue Origin, owns The Washington Post and chairs the Bezos Earth Fund.

bioSource.title: Amazon 2026 proxy statement (Form DEF 14A), director biography

school.name: Day 1: customer-first, long-term invention
school.tagline: Start from the customer, judge choices over years not quarters, and keep a start-up's speed.

principles.name: Customer obsession
principles.summary: He argues that centering a company on customers, rather than on competitors or products, keeps it inventive, because customers always want something better even when they say they are happy. His first letter promised to focus relentlessly on customers.

sources.title: 1997 letter to shareholders (reprinted with the 2017 letter)

principles.name: It's all about the long term
principles.summary: His 1997 letter said Amazon would make investment decisions for long-term market leadership, not short-term profit or Wall Street's reaction, and would choose future cash flow over flattering accounting.

sources.title: 1997 letter to shareholders (reprinted with the 2017 letter)

principles.name: Invent, wander and accept failure
principles.summary: He expects bold bets, many of which will fail, and says failures need to grow in size along with the company. He points to AWS as something no customer asked for, and to the Fire phone as a flop whose lessons and developers sped up work on Echo and Alexa.

sources.title: 1997 letter to shareholders (reprinted with the 2017 letter)

principles.name: Stay in Day 1: decide fast
principles.summary: Day 2, he wrote, is stasis followed by decline. To avoid it he urges making most decisions with about 70% of the information you wish you had, correcting mistakes quickly, and using "disagree and commit" to move ahead without full agreement.

decisions.title: The Wall Street job or the online store?
decisions.situation: You joined investment firm D. E. Shaw & Co. in December 1990 and became a senior vice president in 1992. You have an idea for a company that sells books over the internet.

options.label: Stay at the firm and keep climbing
Quit and start an online bookstore
Build it as a side project, keep the job

decisions.actual: He left D. E. Shaw in June 1994 and founded Amazon.com in July 1994. The site began selling books in July 1995.
decisions.outcome: Amazon went public in May 1997 at $18 a share, after 1996 sales of $15.7 million. For 2025 it reported total net sales of $716.9 billion.

lesson.takeaway: He left a senior job at an established firm to bet on where online shopping could go over many years, not on quick profits.
lesson.watchOut: The early company was fragile: its 1997 IPO prospectus warned of a limited operating history, a $9.0 million accumulated deficit and more losses ahead.

decisions.title: Charge a yearly fee for fast shipping?
decisions.situation: Your store already wins customers with low prices and free shipping. Fast, express delivery is still an extra cost people pay order by order, and giving it away unlimited would be expensive for you in the short term.

options.label: Launch a flat yearly membership with free two-day shipping
Keep charging for express shipping on each order
Offer free express shipping only on big orders

decisions.actual: In February 2005 Amazon launched Amazon Prime, its first membership program: $79 a year for unlimited free two-day shipping with no minimum order. He admitted it would cost the company in the short term.
decisions.outcome: In his shareholder letter published in April 2017 he wrote that no customer ever asked Amazon to create Prime. In his April 2021 letter he said Amazon had more than 200 million Prime members. In 2025 Amazon's subscription sales, which include Prime fees, were $49.6 billion.

sources.title: Amazon.com announces record free cash flow; introduces Amazon Prime

lesson.takeaway: Amazon took on a cost it called expensive in the short term to remove a customer annoyance: minimum orders and waiting to bundle purchases. He later wrote that no customer ever asked for Prime.
lesson.watchOut: Subscriptions can backfire: in September 2025 Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle FTC allegations that it enrolled people in Prime without consent and made cancelling hard.

sources.title: FTC secures historic $2.5 billion settlement against Amazon

decisions.title: Rent out your computer systems?
decisions.situation: You are an online retailer. To run your own websites you have built large, reliable, low-cost data storage systems. Outside software developers could use the same thing.

options.label: Keep the systems in-house as an edge for the store
Sell the same infrastructure to any developer
License the software to big tech companies

decisions.actual: On March 14, 2006 Amazon Web Services launched Amazon S3, a storage service that gave any developer the same infrastructure Amazon used for its own sites.
decisions.outcome: In 2025 AWS sales rose 20% to $128.7 billion, with $45.6 billion in operating income.

lesson.takeaway: Amazon turned tools it built for itself into a product for everyone, a bet he later described as following a hunch that no customer had asked for.
lesson.watchOut: When others run on your systems, your outages become theirs: a command entered with a wrong input on February 28, 2017 took Amazon S3 down for hours in its Northern Virginia region and disrupted other AWS services there.

sources.title: Summary of the Amazon S3 service disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region

decisions.title: Buy a famous newspaper?
decisions.situation: The Washington Post Company, led by chairman Donald Graham, has decided to sell the paper after years of newspaper-industry struggles. Its leaders wonder if another owner might be better for it.

options.label: Pass; newspapers are a shrinking business
Buy it personally, separate from Amazon

decisions.actual: In August 2013 he agreed to buy The Washington Post and related publishing businesses for $250 million, through a company of his own, not Amazon. He asked the paper's top leaders to stay on.
decisions.outcome: The sale closed on October 1, 2013 to his company Nash Holdings. The seller renamed itself Graham Holdings. Amazon's 2026 proxy still lists the Post among the businesses he owns.

sources.title: Jeffrey P. Bezos to purchase The Washington Post (press release, 8-K exhibit)
The Washington Post Company Form 8-K on completion of the sale
The Washington Post Company renamed Graham Holdings

lesson.takeaway: He bought the paper personally and framed its mission around its audience: "Our duty to readers will continue to be the heart of the Post."
lesson.watchOut: An owner's choices can cost reader trust: after the Post said in October 2024 it would not endorse a presidential candidate, a decision Bezos took responsibility for, NPR reported that more than 250,000 subscribers had left.

sources.title: Jeffrey P. Bezos to purchase The Washington Post (press release, 8-K exhibit)
More than 250,000 subscribers have left 'Washington Post' over withheld endorsement

decisions.title: How big a bet on climate?
decisions.situation: You run Amazon, which has just pledged to use 100% renewable energy by 2030 and reach carbon neutrality by 2040. Some Amazon employees have pushed for more. You are deciding how much of your own fortune to put toward climate.

options.label: Pledge $10 billion to a new climate fund
Leave it to Amazon's own climate programs

decisions.actual: On February 17, 2020 he announced the Bezos Earth Fund on Instagram, committing $10 billion of his own money to fund scientists, activists and groups working to protect the natural world.
decisions.outcome: On November 16, 2020 he named the first 16 grantees, sharing $791 million; five groups got $100 million each. Amazon's 2026 proxy says the $10 billion is to be given out as grants within this decade.

sources.title: Amazon's Jeff Bezos pledges $10 billion to launch Earth Fund for combating climate change
Jeff Bezos pledges $10 billion to fight climate change
Jeff Bezos names first recipients of his $10 billion Earth Fund

lesson.takeaway: He committed a large, fixed sum to a problem measured in decades and set a timeframe, this decade, for giving it out.
lesson.watchOut: A pledge is not money spent yet: the first grants in November 2020 totaled $791 million of the $10 billion, with the rest to be granted over the decade.

sources.title: Jeff Bezos names first recipients of his $10 billion Earth Fund

glossary.definition: The first time a company sells its shares to the public.
What a company earned or lost in a period after all its expenses, interest and income taxes are subtracted from its revenue. A profit is called net income (or net profit); a shortfall is a net loss.
The total money a company takes in from selling its goods and services, before any costs are subtracted.
Renting computing power, storage and software over the internet on demand, and paying for what you use, instead of buying and running your own machines.
The profit a business makes from its main activities after paying operating costs, before interest and income taxes.
A report U.S. public companies file with the SEC to announce major events soon after they happen, between their regular annual and quarterly reports.
